$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
n = 28, \qquad
\mu = 8, \qquad
\sigma = 14.
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(8,\frac{{14}^{2}}{28}) \\  & ∼N(8,7).\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162110 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-bab81480-9192-56c0-939c-2fac0be1b0c9"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186161676 :question/problem "Given that $X_1, X_2, \ldots,X_{100} \sim N(-4, 20^2)$ is a random sample of size $100$ from a normal population, calculate $P(-4.3 \lt \overline{X} \lt -3.9).$

*Hint: A value table of $\Phi(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $\Phi(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\, 0.04 \,$ | $\, 0.05 \,$ | $\, 0.06 \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\, -0.1 \,$ | $\, 0.4443 \,$ | $\, 0.4404 \,$ | $\, 0.4364 \,$ |
| $\, 0.0 \,$ | $\, 0.5160 \,$ | $\, 0.5199 \,$ | $\, 0.5239 \,$ |
| $\, 0.1 \,$ | $\, 0.5557 \,$ | $\, 0.5596 \,$ | $\, 0.5636 \,$ |" :question/worked-solution "If $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
X_i \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2), \qquad 1\leq i\leq n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overline{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overline{X} \sim N\left(\mu, \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(-4,\frac{{20}^{2}}{100}) \\  & ∼N(-4,4).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(-4.3 \lt \overline{X} \lt -3.9).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-4.3<\overset{―}{X}<-3.9) & =P(\frac{-4.3-(-4)}{\sqrt{4}}<Z<\frac{-3.9-(-4)}{\sqrt{4}}) \\  & =P(-0.15<Z<0.05) \\  & =Φ(0.05)-Φ(-0.15)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.05)=0.5199, \\ Φ(-0.15)=0.4404.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-0.15<Z<0.05) & =Φ(0.05)-Φ(-0.15) \\  & =0.5199-0.4404 \\  & =0.0795.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162111 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-489fc166-95e5-5a00-b747-9b64225018dc" "question-bf44009c-d977-5a1b-baed-2f30870bd66c" "question-441c8655-31b2-5bd2-b0eb-1aa21153695d" "question-a16286a3-509a-570e-8f6f-6720e9566628"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186161677 :question/problem "The diastolic blood pressure of adult men in a given population is normally distributed with a mean of $75\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}$ and a standard deviation of $10\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}.$ Suppose $10$ men are selected at random. | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

$$
X_i\sim N(\mu, \sigma^2), \qquad 1\leq i\leq n,
$$

 then the sample mean $\overline{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overline{X}\sim N\left(\mu, \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

We're told that the population mean $\mu=75,$ the population standard deviation $\sigma = 10,$ and that the sample size $n=10.$ Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(75,\frac{{10}^{2}}{10}) \\  & ∼N(75,10).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P( \overline{X} \lt 70).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<70) & =P(Z<\frac{70-75}{\sqrt{10}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<-1.58) \\  & =Φ(-1.58)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-1.58) & =0.0571.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<70) & =Φ(-1.58) \\  & =0.0571.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-cc9af1e1-2430-571a-97fc-932c8c2c6f9f" :question/id #uuid "cc9af1e1-2430-571a-97fc-932c8c2c6f9f" :question/math-academy-id "q-143263" :question/problem "Given that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{18}∼N(12,{6}^{2})$ is a random sample of size $n=18$ from a normal population, what is the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}?$" :question/worked-solution "If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where

$$
X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n} \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2).
$$

In this case, we can easily determine the sampling distribution of the sample mean

$$
\overline{X} = \dfrac{1}{n} \sum\limits_{i=1}^n X_i.
$$

Recall the following:

- The sum of $n$ independent and identically distributed normal random variables is normally distributed. Thus, 

$$
Y = \displaystyle \sum\limits_{i=1}^n X_i
$$

is normally distributed.

- A normally distributed random variable scaled by a constant factor is normally distributed. Thus, 

$$
\overline{X} = \dfrac1n\cdot Y
$$

is normally distributed.

Also, we previously saw that the expected value of the sample mean equals the population mean, i.e., 

$$
\textrm{E}[\overline{X}] = \mu,
$$

and the variance of the sample mean is

$$
\textrm{Var}[\overline{X}] = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}.
$$

Putting all of this together, we obtain that

$$
\overline{X} \sim N\left(\mu, \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right),
$$

In other words, the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and variance $\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162197 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

$$

- A normally distributed random variable scaled by a constant factor is normally distributed. Thus, 

$$
\overline{X} = \dfrac1n\cdot Y

$$
\textrm{E}[\overline{X}] = \mu,
$$

and the variance of the sample mean is

$$
\textrm{Var}[\overline{X}] = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}.
$$

Putting all of this together, we obtain that

$$
\overline{X} \sim N\left(\mu, \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right),
$$

$$

$$
\overline{X} = \dfrac{1}{n} \sum\limits_{i=1}^n X_i

$\overline{X} = \dfrac1n\cdot Y$

$$
\textrm{E}[\overline{X}] = \mu
$$

and the variance of the sample mean is

$$
\textrm{Var}[\overline{X}] = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}
$$

Putting all of this together, we obtain that

$$
\overline{X} \sim N\left(\mu, \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)
$$

In other words, the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and variance

$$
\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}
